title: Comet Hale–Bopp
wiki_lead:
Comet Hale–Bopp (formally designated C/1995 O1) is a long-period comet that was one of the most widely observed of the 20th century and one of the brightest seen for many decades.
Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp discovered Comet Hale–Bopp separately on July 23, 1995, before it became visible to the naked eye. It is difficult to predict the maximum brightness of new comets with any degree of certainty, but Hale–Bopp exceeded most predictions when it passed perihelion on April 1, 1997, reaching about magnitude −1.8. Its massive nucleus size made it visible to the naked eye for a record 18 months. This is twice as long as the Great Comet of 1811, the previous record holder. Accordingly, Hale–Bopp was dubbed the Great Comet of 1997.
wiki_excerpt:
Comet Hale–Bopp (formally designated C/1995 O1) is a long-period comet that was one of the most widely observed of the 20th century and one of the brightest seen for many decades.
Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp discovered Comet Hale–Bopp separately on July 23, 1995, before it became visible to the naked eye. It is difficult to predict the maximum brightness of new comets with any degree of certainty, but Hale–Bopp exceeded most predictions when it passed perihelion on April 1, 1997, reaching about magnitude −1.8. Its massive nucleus size made it visible to the naked eye for a record 18 months. This is twice as long as the Great Comet of 1811, the previous record holder. Accordingly, Hale–Bopp was dubbed the Great Comet of 1997.


Discovery
The comet was discovered independently on July 23, 1995, by two observers, Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp, both in the United States.
Hale had spent many hundreds of hours searching for comets without success, and was tracking known comets from his driveway in New Mexico when he chanced upon Hale–Bopp just after midnight. The comet had an apparent magnitude of 10.5 and lay near the globular cluster M70 in the constellation of Sagittarius. Hale first established that there was no other deep-sky object near M70, and then consulted a directory of known comets, finding that none were known to be in this area of the sky. Once he had established that the object was moving relative to the background stars, he emailed the Central Bureau for Astronomical Telegrams, the clearing house for astronomical discoveries, at around 6:50 UT, shortly after his observations.
Bopp did not own a telescope. He was out with friends at Vekol Ranch, about 140 kilometres (90 miles) south of Phoenix (near Stanfield), observing star clusters and galaxies when he chanced across the comet while at the eyepiece of a homemade 44 cm (17.5 in) Dobsonian telescope owned by his friend Jim Stevens. He realized he might have spotted something new when, like Hale, he checked his star maps to determine if any other deep-sky objects were known to be near M70, and found none. He alerted the Central Bureau for Astronomical Telegrams about two hours after Hale through a Western Union telegram. Brian G. Marsden, who had run the bureau since 1968, laughed, "Nobody sends telegrams anymore. I mean, by the time that telegram got here, Alan Hale had already e-mailed us three times with updated coordinates."
The following morning, it was confirmed that this was a new comet, and it was given the designation C/1995 O1. The discovery was announced in International Astronomical Union circular 6187.


Early observation
Hale–Bopp's orbital position was calculated as 7.2 astronomical units (AU) from the Sun, placing it between Jupiter and Saturn and by far the greatest distance from Earth at which a comet had been discovered by amateurs. grok_lead: Comet HaleâBopp, formally designated C/1995 O1, is a long-period comet originating from the Oort Cloud, notable for its large nucleus measuring approximately 37 miles (60 kilometers) in diameter and for being one of the brightest and most widely observed comets of the 20th century. It was discovered independently on July 23, 1995, by amateur astronomers Alan Hale in Cloudcroft, New Mexico, and Thomas Bopp near Stanfield, Arizona, while they were observing the globular cluster M70, at a distance of about 7.15 AU from the Sun. The comet's exceptional brightness allowed it to remain visible to the naked eye for a record 18 months, from May 1996 through October 1997, even in light-polluted urban areas, outshining all other comets since the Great Comet of 1811. HaleâBopp reached perihelion, its closest point to the Sun, on April 1, 1997, at a distance of 0.914 AU, where it exhibited a brilliant coma and multiple tails: a prominent white dust tail, a blue ion tail influenced by the solar wind, and a faint third tail composed of neutral sodium atoms. Its closest approach to Earth occurred on March 22, 1997, at approximately 122 million miles (1.3 AU), providing optimal viewing conditions and enabling extensive observations by ground-based telescopes, spacecraft like NASA's Ulysses, and the Hubble Space Telescope. Following its gravitational interaction with Jupiter in 1996, HaleâBopp has an orbital period of approximately 2,400 years and is not expected to return to the inner Solar System until around the year 4380. The comet's passage sparked intense scientific interest, revealing insights into cometary composition through spectroscopy that detected unprecedented levels of organic molecules and water ice, contributing to understandings of Solar System formation and the delivery of volatiles to early Earth. Its high activity at large distances from the Sunâevident even at discoveryâhighlighted the role of its massive nucleus in producing vast amounts of gas and dust, making it a benchmark for studying long-period comets.
